title: Ranking and Order Advanced: Comparisons, Intersections, and Mixed Lines

questions.question: R is heavier than S but lighter than T; T is lighter than M. If these four are ranked by weight, who is second heaviest?
questions.rationale: Convert: T > R > S and M > T. Merge into M > T > R > S. Second heaviest is T — one inequality per sentence, merged through the shared letter T.

questions.question: A scores more than B; R scores less than S; B scores more than S; T scores less than R. Who stands in the middle of the merged chain?
questions.rationale: Inequalities: A > B, S > R, B > S, R > T. Merge through anchors B and R: A > B > S > R > T. The middle of five is S. Watch the reversed readings: 'R scores less than S' is S > R.

questions.question: In a 9-floor building there are as many floors above X's floor as below Y's. If X lives on floor 3, Y lives on:
questions.rationale: Floors above X: 9 - 3 = 6. Set below-Y count equal: Y - 1 = 6, so Y = 7. The classic slip is writing Y = 6 by counting Y's own floor among 'below'.

questions.question: Six boys face six girls across a table (facing rows). Amit is 3rd from the left among boys. The girl facing him is (from the girls' left, girls facing the boys):
questions.rationale: In facing rows of six, paired positions sum to N + 1: pos_girl = 7 - 3 = 4. The facing convention (each row's 'left' is its own) creates the reversal — extract it from the puzzle text before computing.

questions.question: In a 40-seat row with seats 12 and 27 broken, the person 15th from the left among OCCUPIED seats sits on which seat?
questions.rationale: Seats 1-11 hold occupied persons #1-#11. Seat 12 is broken, so occupied #12 = seat 13, #13 = seat 14, #14 = seat 15, #15 = seat 16 (the second broken seat, 27, is far to the right and does not intervene). Convert person-ranks to seat-ranks by adding one for each broken seat encountered.

questions.question: Five boxes A-E in a stack (bottom = 1): E at the bottom; C second from the top; B above E but below C; D immediately above B; A not adjacent to E. Which box is on top?
questions.rationale: E = 1, C = 4. B is 2 or 3; D immediately above B: if B = 3 then D = 4 (taken), so B = 2, D = 3. The leftover seat 5 goes to A, which is indeed not adjacent to E (1). Top = A. Anchors first, constrained pairs second, leftover verified last.

questions.question: While merging comparison chains you hit an apparent contradiction (X > Y > Z > X). The FIRST thing to do is:
options: Re-check your inequality conversions for a flipped sign
questions.rationale: Genuine cycles almost never appear in exam data — the usual culprit is a reversed reading ('P is smaller than Q' written as P > Q). Audit your own conversions before blaming the paper.

questions.question: In a merit list, P is 5th from the top, Q is three ranks below P, and R is above Q but below P with nobody between R and P. Who is 7th?
questions.rationale: Fixing ranks: R = 6th (immediately below P), Q = 8th. The 7th position belongs to no named person — 'data inadequate' style options reward exact anchoring, and misreading R as 7th is the planted trap.

questions.question: Two parallel queues match people by index (the 4th of queue 1 corresponds to the 4th of queue 2). This differs from facing rows because:
options: Positions match by index instead of summing to N + 1
questions.rationale: Facing rows pair as pos_A + pos_B = N + 1 (reversal); parallel same-direction queues pair equal indices (4th with 4th). The facing convention in the puzzle's own wording decides which equation applies.

questions.question: The core discipline that earns marks in advanced ranking is:
options: Writing every relation as visible arithmetic before answering
questions.rationale: Options in advanced puzzles are engineered to punish chains held only in the head. Inequality-convert, merge via anchors, write balance equations and facing conventions — visible arithmetic, not mental gymnastics.
